notes.title: Is she pregnant? Presumptive, probable, positive

lines.text: A woman has missed her period for 8 weeks, has nausea and breast tenderness. Her urine hCG test is positive.
Presumptive signs = what the WOMAN feels: missed period, nausea, breast changes, urinary frequency, fatigue, quickening (16–18 weeks).
Probable signs = what the EXAMINER finds but other causes are possible: Goodell (soft cervix), Hegar (soft lower segment), Chadwick (bluish vagina), ballottement, Braxton Hicks, positive hCG test.
Positive signs = only 3: fetal heart heard, fetal movements felt by the examiner, fetus seen on ultrasound.
A positive pregnancy test is a PROBABLE sign, not positive: tests are 95–98% accurate.
Urine hCG positive about 14 days after conception.
Fetal heart: ultrasound from 6–7 weeks; fetoscope from 18–20 weeks; normal 120–160/min.
Examiner feels fetal movement from 20–24 weeks.
Which finding is a positive sign of pregnancy?
a. Positive urine hCG test ✗: a probable sign: tests can be wrong.
b. Hegar's sign ✗: a probable sign found by the examiner.
c. Fetal heart beat seen on ultrasound ✓: only the fetus itself proves pregnancy.
d. Quickening felt by the woman ✗: a presumptive sign: subjective.

notes.title: EDD, gestational age, gravida and para

lines.text: A woman with LNMP 10/01/2017 E.C. asks when she will deliver. She has 2 children, 2 stillbirths and 1 abortion.
Pregnancy lasts 280 days (40 weeks) from the first day of the LNMP.
Ethiopian calendar: add 9 months and 10 days to LNMP (9 months and 5 days if Pagume falls in between).
Gregorian calendar (Naegele): add 7 days, subtract 3 months, add 1 year.
Gravida = number of pregnancies including the current one.
Para = number of pregnancies that reached viability (28 weeks in Ethiopia), alive or dead; twins count once.
TPAL: Term (37+ wks), Preterm (28–37), Abortions (before 28 wks), Living children.
Example: 2 children + 2 stillbirths + 1 abortion, now pregnant → gravida 6, para 4.
Gestational age by fundal height: from 20 weeks, cm ≈ weeks (1 cm = 1 week); finger method 1 finger ≈ 2 weeks, less accurate.
A woman with 3 living children (one set of twins among them, born at term), no abortions, is pregnant now. She had 2 deliveries before. What is her gravida and para?
a. G4 P3 ✗: twins count as one delivery for parity.
b. G3 P2 ✓: two previous deliveries (one was twins) plus current pregnancy = G3; para counts deliveries, not babies.
c. G3 P3 ✗: para counts births beyond viability, not number of babies.
d. G2 P2 ✗: the current pregnancy is counted in gravida.
At 36 weeks, a nurse palpates a soft, irregular mass at the fundus and a hard, round, movable part just above the pubis.
1st (fundal): what is in the fundus? Head = hard, round, ballotable; breech = soft, irregular.
2nd (lateral): where is the back? Smooth firm side = back; lumpy side = limbs.
3rd (Pawlik, suprapubic): what is the presenting part and is it engaged?
4th (deep pelvic, facing her feet): is the head flexed or extended?
Lie: longitudinal, oblique or transverse. Presentation: cephalic (vertex best), breech, shoulder.
Hear fetal heart best over the fetal back; check maternal pulse at the same time.
Station 0 = presenting part at the ischial spines; engaged when only 2/5 or less of the head is palpable above the brim.
Ask her to empty the bladder; position supine with knees slightly flexed and head slightly raised.
Inspect for size, shape, skin changes and scars before palpating.
During Leopold's maneuver the nurse feels a hard round movable mass in the fundus. What does this suggest?
a. Vertex presentation ✗: the head would be at the pelvis, not the fundus.
b. Breech presentation ✓: the head is in the fundus, so the buttocks present.
c. Transverse lie ✗: in transverse lie the fundus is empty of poles.
d. Twin pregnancy ✗: one finding does not show twins.

notes.title: Antenatal care: visits, tests, TT, nutrition

lines.text: A 24-year-old comes for her first ANC visit at 10 weeks.
WHO now advises at least 8 ANC contacts, the first before 12 weeks. The older focused model used 4 visits: before 16 wks, 24–28, 32, 36.
Routine tests: Hgb (anemia below 11 g/dl), blood group and Rh, VDRL/syphilis, HIV, HBsAg, urine for protein, sugar, pus cells.
Rh-negative mother: indirect Coombs test, repeated at 28 weeks.
Every pregnant woman: iron + folic acid throughout pregnancy.
Teach danger signs: vaginal bleeding, severe headache, blurred vision, fits, fever, leaking fluid, reduced fetal movement, severe abdominal pain.
TT (Td) schedule: TT1 at first contact; TT2 4 weeks later (protects 3 yrs); TT3 6 months later (5 yrs); TT4 1 year later (10 yrs); TT5 1 year later (lifelong). 0.5 ml IM deltoid.
Recommended weight gain: 11.5–16 kg (average); about 0.4 kg/week in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Underweight gain more, obese less.
Limit caffeine below 150 mg/day; no alcohol.
Exercise 30 minutes daily; sex is safe unless bleeding, leaking or previa.
Wash breasts with water only (no soap); supportive bra.
A pregnant woman received TT1 at her first visit. When is the earliest she can get TT2?
a. After 1 week ✗: too short to build immunity.
b. After 4 weeks ✓: minimum interval between TT1 and TT2 is 4 weeks.
c. After 6 months ✗: that is the interval between TT2 and TT3.
d. After 1 year ✗: that is the interval for TT3 to TT4.
At 10 weeks a woman vomits every morning; at 30 weeks she complains of heartburn and constipation.
Morning sickness affects about 50% and usually settles after the first 3 months.
Vomiting beyond 12–16 weeks or causing weight loss, dehydration, ketones → hyperemesis gravidarum (not minor).
Nausea: dry carbohydrate (crackers) before getting up, small frequent meals, avoid fatty food, vitamin B6.
Heartburn: small frequent meals, do not lie down after eating, sleep with 2 pillows, antacids.
Constipation: fibre, fruits, vegetables, 8 glasses of water; stool softener if needed.
Hemorrhoids: prevent constipation, cold compress, Sims position rest.
Back pain: good posture, low heels; back pain can be an early sign of UTI.
No mineral oil (removes fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K) and no enemas (can start labor).
A pregnant woman with constipation asks about mineral oil. What should the nurse say?
a. It is the best laxative in pregnancy ✗: it removes fat-soluble vitamins.
b. Avoid it; increase fibre and water instead ✓: diet measures are first-line and safe.
c. Use an enema daily ✗: enemas may start labor.
d. Stop iron tablets permanently ✗: iron is needed; manage constipation instead.

notes.title: Normal labor: true vs false, stages and phases

lines.text: A primigravida at 39 weeks has contractions every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds that started in her back. Cervix 5 cm.
True labor: regular contractions that get stronger and closer, start in the back and sweep to the front, continue with walking, and dilate the cervix.
False labor: irregular, felt in the abdomen only, stop with walking or rest, no cervical change.
1st stage: onset of true labor to full dilatation (10 cm): longest stage.
2nd stage: full dilatation to birth of the baby.
3rd stage: birth of baby to delivery of placenta: shortest, but highest PPH risk.
4th stage: first 1–4 hours after the placenta.
Normal labor: spontaneous, term, single, vertex, finished within 24 hours, no complications.
Latent phase: 0–3 cm, mild contractions every 5–20 min lasting 20–40 s.
Active phase: 4–7 cm, contractions every 3–5 min lasting 40–60 s; cervix dilates about 1 cm/hour.
Transition: 8–10 cm, contractions every 2–3 min lasting 60–90 s, urge to push at the end.
2nd stage normally up to 2 hours in nullipara, 1 hour in multipara.
Primigravida: cervix effaces before it dilates; multipara: both happen together.
Signs of labor: regular contractions (surest), show, rupture of membranes.
A woman has irregular contractions felt only in the lower abdomen that stop when she walks. The cervix has not changed. What is this?
a. Active labor ✗: active labor has regular contractions and cervical change.
b. False labor ✓: irregular, abdominal, relieved by walking, no cervical change.
c. Transition phase ✗: transition has strong frequent contractions at 8–10 cm.
d. Second stage ✗: requires full dilatation.

notes.title: Mechanism of labor and the 5 P's

lines.text: During the second stage the head crowns, is born by extension, then turns to face the mother's thigh.
5 P's affecting labor: Passenger, Powers, Passage, Position, Psyche.
Cardinal movements in order: Descent → Flexion → Internal rotation → Extension → External rotation (restitution) → Expulsion.
Flexion shrinks the presenting diameter from about 12 cm to 9.5 cm.
The anterior shoulder is born first, then the posterior.
Upright positions in the 1st stage use gravity and shorten labor; avoid lying flat on the back (supine hypotension).
Fear and tension increase pain and slow labor: support matters.
What is the correct order of the cardinal movements of labor?
a. Flexion, descent, extension, internal rotation ✗: descent comes first; rotation precedes extension.
b. Descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, expulsion ✓: the correct sequence.
c. Descent, extension, flexion, expulsion ✗: extension happens after rotation.
d. Internal rotation, descent, flexion, expulsion ✗: descent begins the process.

notes.title: Partograph: reading alert and action lines

lines.text: A woman admitted at 4 cm has her cervicogram crossing to the right of the alert line.
Start plotting in the active phase (4 cm).
Alert line: from 4 cm, expected progress of 1 cm/hour. Crossing it → more watchful care, look for cause, consider referral.
Action line: 4 hours to the right of the alert line. Crossing it → act: assess for CPD/malpresentation, augment or cesarean.
Amniotic fluid codes: I = intact, C = clear, M = meconium, B = blood-stained.
Moulding: 1 = sutures touching, 2 = overlapped but reducible, 3 = overlapped not reducible (danger).
FHR and contractions every 30 min; pulse every 30 min; BP every 4 h; temperature every 2 h; vaginal exam every 4 h; urine each time passed.
Contractions: count how many in 10 minutes and how long each lasts (under 20 s, 20–40 s, over 40 s).
On a partograph the cervicogram crosses the action line. What does this mean?
a. Labor is progressing normally ✗: normal progress stays left of the alert line.
b. Labor is abnormal: urgent assessment and intervention needed ✓: crossing the action line means 4 hours behind expected progress.
c. The woman is in the latent phase ✗: the partograph tracks the active phase.
d. The baby will be born in 1 hour ✗: no such meaning.

notes.title: Third stage: AMTSL and checking the placenta

lines.text: A baby has just been born. The nurse confirms there is no second baby.
Active management of the third stage (AMTSL) prevents PPH: 1) uterotonic within 1 minute of birth (oxytocin 10 IU IM), 2) controlled cord traction, 3) uterine massage after the placenta.
Exclude a second baby before giving oxytocin.
Signs of separation: uterus becomes globular and rises, cord lengthens, gush of blood.
CCT: one hand above the pubis pushes the uterus upward (counter-traction) while the other pulls the cord down and back, during a contraction; never jerk.
Examine the placenta: cotyledons complete, membranes complete, 3 cord vessels (2 arteries, 1 vein).
Normal blood loss 300–500 ml.
Misoprostol 600 mcg orally if oxytocin is not available.
Ergometrine raises BP: not in hypertension/preeclampsia or heart disease.
CCT without counter-traction can invert the uterus.
Which is the first step of active management of the third stage of labor?
a. Pull the cord immediately after birth ✗: uterotonic and contraction come first; counter-traction is needed.
b. Give oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute after birth (after excluding another baby) ✓: the uterotonic is the most important step.
c. Massage the uterus before the baby is born ✗: massage follows placental delivery.
d. Wait 1 hour for the placenta ✗: that is expectant management, with more bleeding.

notes.title: Monitoring in labor: maternal and fetal danger signs

lines.text: During labor the FHR is 96/min and the liquor is thick green.
FHR outside 110–160/min is abnormal; above 180 or below 100/min → fetal distress.
Meconium-stained liquor → fetal hypoxia (except in breech presentation).
Maternal BP 140/90 or more → report (preeclampsia); falling BP or pulse above 100 → possible hemorrhage.
Contractions becoming weaker or shorter → uterine inertia; no relaxation between contractions → danger to fetus.
Bandl's (pathological retraction) ring across the abdomen → obstructed labor, impending uterine rupture.
Fetal distress: turn to left side, stop oxytocin, give oxygen and IV fluids, call for help, prepare for quick delivery.
Encourage walking until membranes rupture; empty bladder every 2–4 hours; continuous support.
During labor a nurse finds FHR 98/min after contractions and meconium-stained fluid. What should she do first?
a. Continue routine observation ✗: these are signs of fetal distress.
b. Turn the mother to her left side, stop oxytocin, give oxygen and inform the midwife/doctor ✓: improves placental flow and starts urgent care.
c. Encourage pushing at 6 cm ✗: pushing before full dilatation is harmful.
d. Give pethidine ✗: sedation does not treat fetal hypoxia.
After a fast delivery a woman has a tear from the vagina through the perineal muscles, but the anal sphincter is intact.
Episiotomy only when indicated (instrumental delivery, fetal distress, rigid perineum), cut at crowning during a contraction.
Mediolateral (45°): less risk to the anal sphincter but more bleeding and pain. Midline: heals easily but can extend into the anus.
Tears: 1st degree = skin and vaginal mucosa; 2nd = perineal muscles; 3rd = reaches the anal sphincter; 4th = into the rectal mucosa.
Uterus firm but bright bleeding continues → suspect a laceration (cervix, vagina, perineum).
Infiltrate lidocaine 1% before cutting/repair; repair with 2/0 chromic catgut.
3rd/4th degree: repair by an experienced provider; stool softener and high-fluid diet.
Perineal care: clean front to back, sitz bath, ice in first 24 hours.
A woman bleeds bright red steadily after birth though her uterus is firm and well contracted. What is the likely cause?
a. Uterine atony ✗: the uterus would be soft and boggy.
b. Genital tract laceration ✓: a firm uterus with bright bleeding suggests a tear.
c. Normal lochia ✗: lochia is not steady bright bleeding.
d. Retained placenta ✗: would usually give a soft uterus.
At 1 minute a baby has a pink body with blue hands and feet, HR 110, grimaces, some flexion and a weak cry.
Steps: dry and wrap (keep warm) → assess breathing → clamp/tie cord → skin-to-skin and breastfeed within 1 hour → eye ointment → vitamin K → weigh.
Not breathing or gasping after drying → start resuscitation (bag and mask) within the first minute.
APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (0–2 each).
7–10 normal; 4–6 moderate asphyxia (clear airway, oxygen); 0–3 severe (immediate resuscitation).
Heat loss: evaporation (wet skin), conduction (cold surface), convection (draught), radiation (cold walls nearby).
Vitamin K 1 mg IM in the thigh (0.5 mg if preterm); tie cord 2 fingers from the abdomen.
Newborn danger signs: RR ≥60 or ≤30, grunting, chest indrawing, poor sucking, temp below 35.5 or 37.5+ °C, convulsions, jaundice in first 24 h, pus from eyes, no stool in 24 h.
Do not bathe in the first 24 hours; leave vernix on.
A newborn at 1 minute: pink body with blue extremities, HR 110, grimace, some flexion, weak irregular cry. What is the APGAR score?
a. 4 ✗: too low; count each sign.
b. 6 ✓: appearance 1 + pulse 2 + grimace 1 + activity 1 + respiration 1 = 6.
c. 8 ✗: would need vigorous cry or active motion.
d. 10 ✗: requires all signs scored 2.
On day 2 after delivery a mother has red lochia and cramps while breastfeeding. Fundus is firm 2 fingers below the umbilicus.
Puerperium lasts 6 weeks.
Fundus at the umbilicus after delivery, descends about 1 cm/day; not palpable abdominally after about 10–14 days.
Lochia: rubra (red, days 1–3/4) → serosa (pinkish-yellow) → alba (white). Never foul-smelling; never pure blood.
Afterpains are normal, stronger in multiparas and during breastfeeding (oxytocin).
Soft, high uterus with persistent lochia → subinvolution (retained tissue, infection).
Blood clots more easily for weeks → DVT risk: early walking.
Check bleeding and uterine tone every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours.
Breastfeed within 1 hour, on demand every 2–3 hours; exclusive for 6 months.
Teach danger signs: fever, heavy bleeding, foul lochia, headache, blurred vision, breast pain, calf pain.
Encourage voiding: a full bladder pushes the uterus up and causes bleeding.
On day 3 postpartum, which finding needs reporting?
a. Red lochia with small clots ✗: normal lochia rubra in the first days.
b. Foul-smelling lochia and fever ✓: suggests puerperal infection.
c. Afterpains during breastfeeding ✗: normal oxytocin effect.
d. Fundus 3 cm below the umbilicus ✗: normal involution.

notes.title: PMTCT: HIV in pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding

lines.text: A pregnant woman tests HIV positive at her first ANC visit.
Transmission: pregnancy 5–10%, labor and delivery 10–20% (highest), breastfeeding 5–10%.
Start lifelong ART for every HIV-positive pregnant or breastfeeding woman the same day (option B+); current first-line is dolutegravir-based (TLD).
High viral load is the biggest risk factor.
Labor: avoid unnecessary ARM, episiotomy, instrumental delivery and prolonged rupture of membranes (over 4 h increases risk).
Infant: nevirapine daily for 6 weeks (high-risk infants: AZT + NVP).
Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while the mother is on ART; no mixed feeding.
Also give: iron-folate, TT, ITN for malaria, cotrimoxazole if indicated, screen for TB and STIs.
Link mother and baby to follow-up; early infant diagnosis (DNA PCR at 6 weeks).
An HIV-positive mother on ART asks how to feed her baby. What is the best advice?
a. Mixed feeding with formula and breast milk ✗: mixed feeding increases transmission risk.
b. Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while continuing ART ✓: safe and protects the baby when the mother is on ART.
c. Stop ART while breastfeeding ✗: ART must continue to protect mother and baby.
d. Never breastfeed ✗: exclusive breastfeeding is recommended unless replacement feeding is AFASS.

notes.title: Natural family planning, LAM and withdrawal

lines.text: A woman's last six cycles were 21, 25, 32, 24, 28 and 34 days. She wants to use the calendar method.
Calendar method: first fertile day = shortest cycle − 18; last fertile day = longest cycle − 11. Works only with regular cycles.
Ovulation signs: temperature rises about 0.5 °C, cervical mucus becomes clear and stretchy.
LAM is 98% effective only if ALL 3: exclusive breastfeeding day and night, no return of periods, baby under 6 months.
Withdrawal often fails (up to 15%): pre-ejaculate contains sperm.
Example: 21 − 18 = day 3; 34 − 11 = day 23 → avoid sex from day 3 to day 23 (wide because cycles are irregular).
A breastfeeding mother using LAM tells you her baby is now 7 months old. What should the nurse advise?
a. Continue LAM, it is still reliable ✗: LAM is reliable only until 6 months.
b. Start another method now ✓: after 6 months LAM no longer protects.
c. Stop breastfeeding ✗: breastfeeding should continue.
d. Use the calendar method immediately ✗: cycles may not be regular yet; choose a reliable method.

notes.title: Hormonal contraception: who can use what

lines.text: A 3-month postpartum breastfeeding mother wants a pill.

Combined pills (estrogen + progestin): prevent ovulation; 99% if taken correctly. Not for breastfeeding mothers under 6 months, smokers over 35, history of clots, liver disease, high BP, unexplained bleeding.
Missed COC more than 12 hours, vomiting or diarrhea → use backup protection.
Progestin-only pill (minipill): safe in breastfeeding; must be taken at the SAME time daily (within 3 hours).
DMPA injection every 3 months (8–12 weeks): irregular bleeding then amenorrhea, weight gain; fertility may take a year to return.
Implants: Implanon 1 rod = 3 years; Jadelle 2 rods = 5 years; most effective and immediately reversible.
Emergency contraception: pills up to 5 days (120 h) after unprotected sex (sooner is better); copper IUD within 5 days is most effective.
Rifampicin and some anti-epileptics reduce pill effectiveness.
A breastfeeding mother 6 weeks after birth wants an oral contraceptive. Which is most appropriate?
a. Combined oral contraceptive ✗: estrogen reduces milk supply; avoid before 6 months of breastfeeding.
b. Progestin-only pill ✓: no estrogen; safe during breastfeeding.
c. No contraception needed while breastfeeding ✗: partial breastfeeding does not protect reliably.
d. Emergency pills monthly ✗: not a regular method.
A woman with 4 children wants a long-acting method without hormones.
Copper IUCD: up to 10–12 years, immediately reversible, no hormones; can be inserted right after delivery or within 48 hours.
IUCD side effects: heavier, more painful periods in the first 3–6 months.
Condoms are the only method that also protects against STIs/HIV.
Diaphragm stays in for at least 6 hours after sex, used with spermicide.
Vasectomy is not effective immediately: use another method until 2 negative semen tests (about 3 months).
Tubal ligation: permanent; counsel carefully.
IUCD: teach to feel for the strings after each period; report fever, abnormal discharge, pelvic pain (PID) or missing strings.
A man asks if he can stop other contraception the day after his vasectomy. What should the nurse say?
a. Yes, it works immediately ✗: sperm remain in the tubes for weeks.
b. Use another method until two semen tests show no sperm ✓: confirmation takes about 3 months.
c. Only for 1 week ✗: too short.
d. Vasectomy does not prevent pregnancy ✗: it is highly effective once confirmed.

notes.title: Placenta previa: painless bright red bleeding

lines.text: At 32 weeks a grand multipara with a previous cesarean has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Uterus soft, FHR normal, presenting part high.
Antepartum hemorrhage (APH) = bleeding after 28 weeks (in Ethiopia) and before birth.
Previa = placenta lies over or near the internal os. Painless, bright red, recurrent bleeding; soft non-tender uterus; often malpresentation.
Risks: high parity, older age, previous cesarean or curettage, twins, smoking.
Grades: 1 low-lying, 2 marginal, 3 partial, 4 complete. Grades 3–4 → cesarean.
NEVER do a vaginal or rectal examination in suspected previa: it can cause massive bleeding.
Bed rest on her side, IV line, blood for Hgb, group and cross-match; vital signs every 5–15 minutes; weigh pads.
Diagnose with ultrasound.
Bleeding stopped, fetus under 36 weeks, mother and baby stable → expectant care; heavy bleeding or labor → deliver regardless of gestational age.
High PPH risk after delivery: the lower segment contracts poorly; also placenta accreta.
A woman at 34 weeks has painless bright red bleeding. What should the nurse avoid?
a. Checking vital signs ✗: needed to detect shock.
b. Digital vaginal examination ✓: may tear the placenta and cause massive hemorrhage.
c. Starting an IV line ✗: needed for fluids and blood.
d. Monitoring fetal heart rate ✗: essential to assess the fetus.

notes.title: Placental abruption: painful bleeding, hard uterus

lines.text: A woman with severe preeclampsia at 36 weeks has sudden severe abdominal pain, a hard tender uterus, small dark bleeding, and signs of shock.
Abruption = placenta separates before the baby is born.
Painful, dark bleeding; board-like, tender uterus; fetal distress or death.
Shock may be out of proportion to visible bleeding: the blood can be concealed behind the placenta.
Risks: hypertension/preeclampsia (main), trauma, high parity, short cord, polyhydramnios, smoking, cocaine.
Complications: DIC, renal failure, PPH, fetal death.
Left lateral position, oxygen, two large IV lines, blood cross-match, vital signs every 5–15 minutes, monitor FHR.
Check clotting (platelets, fibrinogen) for DIC.
No vaginal exam or enema.
Deliver: cesarean if baby alive and distressed; vaginal if baby dead or delivery is near.
Which finding best differentiates abruptio placenta from placenta previa?
a. Bright red painless bleeding ✗: typical of previa.
b. Painful, rigid, tender uterus ✓: typical of abruption.
c. Soft uterus ✗: seen in previa.
d. Malpresentation ✗: more common in previa.

notes.title: Too much or too little amniotic fluid

lines.text: At 30 weeks a diabetic woman's uterus is much larger than dates, tense, fetal parts are hard to feel and she is breathless. AFI is 28 cm.
Polyhydramnios: AFI over 25 cm, deepest pocket over 8 cm, or volume over 2 L.
Causes of poly: diabetes, fetal swallowing problems (anencephaly, esophageal atresia), twins, Rh disease.
Risks of poly: preterm labor, cord prolapse when membranes rupture, abruption, PPH.
Oligohydramnios: AFI below 5 cm, deepest pocket under 2 cm, or under 500 ml.
Causes of oligo: ruptured membranes (commonest), fetal kidney problems, post-term, placental insufficiency.
Risks of oligo: lung hypoplasia, limb/face deformities, cord compression, IUGR.
Normal AFI 5–25 cm; normal deepest pocket 2–8 cm; term volume about 800–1000 ml.
Poly: rest, report leaking fluid immediately (cord prolapse risk), avoid constipation; amnioreduction if severe.
Oligo: hydrate the mother, frequent fetal surveillance.
A pregnant woman's AFI is 3 cm at 38 weeks. What is this called?
a. Normal amniotic fluid ✗: normal is 5–25 cm.
b. Oligohydramnios ✓: AFI below 5 cm.
c. Polyhydramnios ✗: AFI above 25 cm.
d. Hydrops ✗: a fetal condition, not an AFI value.
At 32 weeks a woman reports a gush of fluid from the vagina followed by continuous leaking. No contractions.
PROM = membranes rupture at least 1 hour before labor starts; PPROM = before 37 weeks.
Main risks: infection (chorioamnionitis), cord prolapse, preterm birth.
Confirm by sterile speculum: pool of fluid, ask her to cough.
Signs of chorioamnionitis: maternal fever, fast pulse, tender uterus, foul-smelling fluid, fetal tachycardia → IV antibiotics and deliver regardless of gestational age.
AVOID digital vaginal exams: they introduce infection.
Term (37+ wks): deliver/induce; antibiotics if ruptured over 12 hours.
Under 34 weeks, no infection: expectant care → bed rest, steroids, prophylactic antibiotics (amoxicillin + erythromycin), check temperature and FHR.
Betamethasone 12 mg IM, 2 doses 24 hours apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg × 4 doses 12 h apart) to mature fetal lungs.
A woman at 31 weeks has PROM without signs of infection. Which action is contraindicated?
a. Giving betamethasone ✗: matures fetal lungs; recommended.
b. Repeated digital vaginal examinations ✓: increase the risk of ascending infection.
c. Monitoring maternal temperature ✗: detects chorioamnionitis early.
d. Giving prophylactic antibiotics ✗: recommended in expectant management.
At 30 weeks a woman has 4 contractions in 20 minutes; cervix 2 cm, membranes intact.
Preterm labor: before 37 completed weeks; 4 contractions in 20 minutes with cervical change.
Associated with UTI, chorioamnionitis, dehydration, adolescents, poor ANC, heavy work.
Try to stop labor only if membranes intact, no bleeding, no fetal distress, cervix under 4–5 cm.
Bed rest on the side, IV hydration, treat infection, tocolytic (nifedipine, terbutaline) as ordered.
Give corticosteroids (betamethasone) between 28 and 34 weeks to mature the lungs.
If labor cannot be stopped: continuous monitoring, prepare newborn resuscitation and warmth.
Why is betamethasone given to a woman in preterm labor at 30 weeks?
a. To stop contractions ✗: it is not a tocolytic.
b. To speed fetal lung maturity ✓: reduces respiratory distress syndrome.
c. To treat infection ✗: it is a steroid, not an antibiotic.
d. To lower blood pressure ✗: no such effect.
At 34 weeks a woman with chronic hypertension has fundal height of 29 cm. Ultrasound shows a small abdomen with normal head size.
IUGR/SGA: below the 10th percentile for gestational age. LBW = under 2500 g; VLBW = under 1500 g.
Asymmetric IUGR (70–80%): head spared, late, from placental insufficiency (hypertension, preeclampsia, anemia, malnutrition).
Symmetric IUGR: all proportionally small, early (chromosomal, infection).
Fundal height 3 cm or more below dates → suspect IUGR; confirm with ultrasound.
Newborn risks: hypoglycemia, hypothermia, polycythemia, asphyxia.
Fetal death: absent fetal movements and no heartbeat on ultrasound; risk of DIC if retained.
IUGR newborn: keep warm, check glucose early, feed early.
After IUFD: check clotting, induce labor if it does not start, watch for PPH, support grieving.
A newborn with IUGR is 2 hours old and jittery. What should the nurse check first?
a. Blood glucose ✓: IUGR babies have low glycogen stores and develop hypoglycemia.
b. Hearing ✗: not urgent.
c. Hip dysplasia ✗: not related to jitteriness.
d. Bilirubin ✗: jaundice is not the first concern at 2 hours.
A woman is at 41 weeks + 3 days by an early ultrasound.
Post-term = beyond 42 completed weeks. Risks: oligohydramnios, placental insufficiency, macrosomia, meconium aspiration, CPD.
Confirm dates (early ultrasound, LNMP, quickening); induce at 41 completed weeks if no contraindication.
Twins: higher risk of preeclampsia, anemia, polyhydramnios, preterm labor, malpresentation, cord prolapse, PPH.
Twins: deliver in hospital by 40 weeks; vaginal if first twin is vertex; cesarean if first twin is not vertex.
Monozygotic (identical) from one ovum; dizygotic (fraternal) from two ova, always 2 placentas.
Twins: watch for PPH after delivery (over-stretched uterus); oxytocin after the last baby.
In a twin delivery, which situation is an indication for cesarean section?
a. Both twins vertex ✗: vaginal delivery is recommended.
b. First twin breech ✓: a non-vertex first twin → cesarean.
c. First twin vertex, second breech ✗: vaginal for twin A, then assisted breech/version for twin B.
d. Mother is a multipara ✗: not an indication.
A primigravida at 34 weeks has BP 165/112, proteinuria 3+, severe headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain.
Hypertension in pregnancy: 140/90 or more on 2 readings at least 4–6 hours apart, or a single 160/110.
Gestational hypertension: after 20 weeks, no proteinuria. Preeclampsia: hypertension + proteinuria after 20 weeks.
Severe preeclampsia: BP 160/110 or more, or proteinuria 3+, or any symptom: severe headache, blurred vision, epigastric/RUQ pain, oliguria (under 400 ml/24 h), pulmonary edema, HELLP, low platelets.
Chronic hypertension: before 20 weeks or persisting beyond 12 weeks postpartum.
Risk: first pregnancy, age under 20 or over 40, twins, diabetes, kidney disease, molar pregnancy, previous preeclampsia.
Mild (under 37 wks): follow up twice weekly, BP, urine protein, fetal growth; teach danger signs; normal diet with no salt restriction.
Severe: admit, MgSO4 to prevent fits, antihypertensive (hydralazine 5–10 mg IV or nifedipine) to keep diastolic under 110, deliver once stable regardless of gestational age.
Left lateral position, catheter, urine output at least 30 ml/hour, strict input/output.
Mild preeclampsia oral drug: methyldopa.
Delivery is the only cure.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in preeclampsia (raises BP): use oxytocin for the third stage.
Edema of legs alone is common in pregnancy; edema of face and hands is more significant.
A woman at 35 weeks has BP 168/114 and proteinuria 3+ with severe headache. What drug is given to prevent convulsions?
a. Diazepam as first choice ✗: a second-line option; causes neonatal depression.
b. Magnesium sulfate ✓: drug of choice to prevent and treat eclamptic fits.
c. Ergometrine ✗: raises BP; contraindicated.
d. Furosemide ✗: does not prevent seizures.
A woman with severe preeclampsia suddenly has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
Eclampsia = fits in a woman with preeclampsia; 50% before labor, 30% in labor, 20% after delivery.
Priorities: protect airway, control fits (MgSO4), control BP, deliver within 12 hours regardless of gestational age.
During the fit: do not leave her, turn on the left side, protect from injury, suction, oxygen 4–6 L/min; do not put anything in the mouth during the fit.
Loading dose: 4 g MgSO4 (20%) IV over 5 minutes + 10 g (50%) deep IM, 5 g in each buttock with 1 ml 2% lidocaine.
Maintenance: 5 g (50%) IM every 4 hours, alternate buttocks, until 24 hours after delivery or the last fit.
If fits recur after 15 minutes: 2 g (50%) IV over 5 minutes.
Before each dose check: respiration at least 16/min, patellar reflexes present, urine at least 100 ml in 4 hours (25–30 ml/h).
Toxicity: RR below 12 or absent reflexes → stop MgSO4 and give calcium gluconate 1 g (10 ml of 10%) IV slowly.
Newborn of a mother on MgSO4: watch for breathing depression and floppiness.
Before giving the next MgSO4 maintenance dose, the nurse finds RR 10/min and absent knee reflexes. What should she do?
a. Give the dose as scheduled ✗: these are signs of magnesium toxicity.
b. Withhold MgSO4 and give calcium gluconate as ordered ✓: calcium gluconate is the antidote.
c. Double the next dose ✗: would worsen toxicity.
d. Give diazepam ✗: would further depress breathing.
An Rh-negative woman married to an Rh-positive man has just delivered an Rh-positive baby.
Problem only when mother is Rh negative and baby is Rh positive.
First pregnancy usually not affected: she becomes sensitized; antibodies attack the next Rh-positive baby (hemolytic disease, hydrops).
Sensitizing events: delivery, abortion, ectopic, amniocentesis, abruption, trauma, wrong blood transfusion.
Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours of any sensitizing event (also routinely at 28 weeks where available).
Indirect Coombs test checks if the mother already has antibodies (at booking and 28 weeks).
An Rh-negative mother delivered an Rh-positive baby and her indirect Coombs test is negative. When should anti-D be given?
a. Before the next pregnancy only ✗: too late; sensitization happens now.
b. Within 72 hours after delivery ✓: prevents antibody formation.
c. Only if the baby is jaundiced ✗: it protects future pregnancies, not this baby.
d. Never, because Coombs is negative ✗: negative Coombs means she is not yet sensitized; give anti-D.
At 11 weeks a woman cannot keep any food or fluid down, has lost 4 kg, dry mouth, and ketones in urine.
Severe vomiting causing dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss → hyperemesis gravidarum.
More common with high hCG: twins, molar pregnancy.
Untreated: electrolyte imbalance, IUGR, preterm birth.
Admit; nothing by mouth for about 24 hours; IV fluids (e.g., 3 L Ringer's with vitamin B).
Antiemetic (metoclopramide), strict input/output including vomitus, daily weight, check urine ketones.
Reintroduce small amounts of clear fluids, then dry carbohydrates every 2–3 hours.
A woman with hyperemesis gravidarum is admitted. What is the initial management?
a. Encourage large meals ✗: will provoke vomiting.
b. Withhold oral intake and give IV fluids with vitamins ✓: rests the gut and corrects dehydration.
c. Give only oral fluids ✗: she cannot keep them down.
d. Discharge with advice ✗: she is dehydrated and ketotic.
At 28 weeks a woman with hookworm and short birth interval has Hgb 8.5 g/dl, pallor and tiredness.
Anemia in pregnancy: Hgb below 11 g/dl (1st and 3rd trimester), below 10.5 in the 2nd.
80–95% is iron deficiency; also folate deficiency.
Causes: poor diet, short birth spacing, heavy periods, hookworm, malaria, bleeding.
Risks: preterm birth, LBW, heart failure in labor, PPH, infection.
Ferrous sulfate 300 mg three times daily; continue 3 months after Hgb normal.
Folic acid 5 mg for megaloblastic anemia.
Deworm (mebendazole after 1st trimester), treat malaria, use bed nets, iron-rich diet, family planning.
Transfuse if Hgb very low (e.g., under 6–7 g/dl in labor) or heart failure.
What is the most common cause of anemia in pregnancy?
a. Vitamin B12 deficiency ✗: uncommon.
b. Iron deficiency ✓: accounts for 80–95% of cases.
c. Sickle cell disease ✗: uncommon cause.
d. Thalassemia ✗: uncommon in Ethiopia.
At 26 weeks an obese woman with a previous 4.5 kg baby has a 1-hour 50 g glucose screen of 160 mg/dl.
Screen at 24–28 weeks: 50 g glucose, 1-hour value over 135–140 mg/dl → do full OGTT.
Pregnancy hormones (HPL, cortisol, estrogen, progesterone) increase insulin resistance.
Baby: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, polyhydramnios, congenital anomalies, stillbirth, newborn hypoglycemia and RDS.
Mother: preeclampsia, infections (candida, UTI), operative delivery.
Diet first; insulin if glucose stays high. Oral hypoglycemics are avoided in pregnancy.
Check the newborn's glucose early and feed early.
Repeat 75 g OGTT 6–12 weeks after delivery; higher lifelong risk of type 2 diabetes.
A baby of a diabetic mother is 1 hour old. Which complication should the nurse watch for first?
a. Hyperglycemia ✗: the baby's high insulin causes LOW glucose.
b. Hypoglycemia ✓: fetal hyperinsulinemia continues after the glucose supply stops.
c. Hypertension ✗: not typical.
d. Post-maturity ✗: not related.
A woman in labor for 20 hours at home arrives dehydrated with strong contractions, the head not descending, heavy moulding and caput, and a ring across the lower abdomen.
Causes of abnormal labor = 3 P's: Powers (weak or uncoordinated contractions), Passage (CPD), Passenger (malposition/malpresentation, big baby).
Obstructed labor: no descent despite strong contractions → CPD, brow/shoulder presentation, hydrocephalus.
Late signs: caput and moulding grade 3, fetal distress, Bandl's ring, uterus fails to relax → impending rupture.
Prolonged latent phase: over 20 h (nullipara) or 14 h (multipara). Prolonged active phase: under 1 cm/hour.
Prolonged 2nd stage: over 2 hours (nullipara) or 1 hour (multipara).
IV fluids for dehydration, blood group and cross-match, catheterize, antibiotics.
Obstructed labor with a live baby → cesarean section as soon as possible. Never augment with oxytocin.
Prolonged 2nd stage with head at 0/5–1/5 → vacuum or forceps; head 2/5 or higher → cesarean.
Complications: uterine rupture, vesicovaginal fistula, infection, PPH, stillbirth, newborn brain damage.
A woman with obstructed labor has a Bandl's ring and fetal distress. What is the correct management?
a. Start oxytocin augmentation ✗: dangerous: can rupture the uterus.
b. Rehydrate, catheterize, antibiotics and immediate cesarean section ✓: relieves obstruction safely.
c. Wait 4 more hours ✗: delay risks rupture and fetal death.
d. Apply fundal pressure ✗: can rupture the uterus.

notes.title: Induction and augmentation: Bishop score and oxytocin

lines.text: A woman at 41+ weeks: cervix 1 cm, 30% effaced, firm, posterior, station −2.
Bishop score: dilatation, effacement, station, consistency, position (0–13).
Score 9 or more (favorable) → oxytocin alone. Below 9 → ripen first with misoprostol 25 mcg vaginally every 4–6 hours or a Foley catheter.
Indications: post-term, severe preeclampsia, PROM, diabetes, IUFD.
Contraindications: placenta previa, transverse lie, cord prolapse, CPD, active genital herpes, previous classical scar.
Oxytocin in IV fluid, start low and increase every 20–40 minutes until 3–5 contractions in 10 minutes each lasting 40–60 s.
Someone stays at the bedside; check FHR, contractions, pulse and BP every 15–30 minutes.
Too many/too long contractions or fetal distress → STOP the infusion, left lateral, oxygen, call for help.
Start oxytocin 6–12 hours after the last prostaglandin dose.
Oxytocin complications: hyperstimulation, fetal distress, uterine rupture, water intoxication, PPH.
Failed induction: no established labor after 6 hours at maximum dose.
During oxytocin infusion, contractions come every 90 seconds lasting 90 seconds and FHR drops to 95. What should the nurse do first?
a. Increase the oxytocin rate ✗: worsens hyperstimulation.
b. Stop the oxytocin infusion ✓: removes the cause of hyperstimulation and fetal distress.
c. Ask her to push ✗: she may not be fully dilated; does not treat the cause.
d. Lay her flat on her back ✗: supine position reduces placental flow.

notes.title: Malpresentations: OP, face, brow, breech, transverse

lines.text: At 38 weeks the fetal head is felt in the fundus and the FHR is heard above the umbilicus.
Occiput posterior: long labor and backache; most rotate; deep transverse arrest or persistent OP may need cesarean.
Brow presentation: largest diameter → cannot deliver vaginally (live baby) → cesarean.
Face: chin anterior can deliver vaginally; chin (mentum) posterior → cesarean.
Transverse lie at term → cesarean (after trying external version before labor).
Breech: fetal head in the fundus, FHR heard high; frank (legs extended), complete (flexed), footling.
Breech risks: cord prolapse, head entrapment, birth injury; planned cesarean is usual.
Breech vaginal birth: hands off until the umbilicus is born; deliver the head with flexion (Mauriceau), never pull.
Compound presentation with prolapsed hand: often delivers vaginally; watch for cord prolapse.
Which presentation at term with a live fetus requires cesarean section?
a. Occiput anterior vertex ✗: the ideal presentation.
b. Brow presentation ✓: presents the largest diameter; vaginal delivery is not possible.
c. Face presentation with chin anterior ✗: can deliver vaginally.
d. Occiput posterior in good labor ✗: most rotate and deliver.

notes.title: Shoulder dystocia, cord prolapse, uterine inversion

lines.text: After the head of a 4.5 kg baby is born, it pulls back against the perineum (turtle sign) and the shoulders do not deliver.
Shoulder dystocia: risk with macrosomia, diabetes, post-term, obesity.
Uterine inversion: sudden heavy bleeding and shock, no fundus palpable, mass in the vagina; caused by cord traction on a relaxed uterus or fundal pressure.
Cord prolapse: cord in front of the presenting part after membranes rupture → emergency; risk with polyhydramnios, malpresentation, high presenting part.
Shoulder dystocia: call for help; McRoberts (thighs pulled to abdomen) + suprapubic pressure; NO fundal pressure.
Cord prolapse: push the presenting part up off the cord with a gloved hand, knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, do not handle the cord, urgent cesarean.
Uterine inversion: do not pull the placenta off, stop oxytocin, call for help, treat shock; the uterus is replaced under relaxation then oxytocin is given.
During labor the membranes rupture and the nurse sees the umbilical cord at the vulva. What is the first action?
a. Push the cord back into the vagina ✗: handling causes spasm and does not relieve compression.
b. Relieve pressure on the cord by lifting the presenting part and positioning knee-chest ✓: keeps blood flowing through the cord.
c. Ask the woman to push hard ✗: increases cord compression.
d. Start oxytocin ✗: worsens compression.
A woman with one previous lower-segment cesarean asks if she can deliver vaginally.
Before vacuum/forceps: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, empty bladder, vertex at station 0 or below, live baby, consent.
Vacuum: only vertex, not before 34 weeks; max 3 pulls, 20–30 minutes, 2 pop-offs.
Most common cesarean indications: fetal distress, CPD, previous cesarean.
VBAC possible after ONE previous low transverse cesarean, no recurring indication, in a facility that can do emergency cesarean.
No VBAC: classical or T-scar, previous myomectomy, estimated weight 4000 g or more, contracted pelvis, malpresentation.
Signs of scar rupture: pain over the scar, maternal tachycardia, fetal distress, poor progress, vaginal bleeding.
A woman with a previous cesarean is in labor and develops pain over the scar, rising pulse and fetal bradycardia. What should the nurse suspect?
a. Normal labor pain ✗: scar pain with tachycardia and fetal distress is not normal.
b. Impending uterine rupture ✓: classic signs of scar rupture.
c. False labor ✗: would not cause fetal distress.
d. Urinary tract infection ✗: does not cause these signs.
Twenty minutes after delivering twins, a woman soaks pads with blood; the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus.
PPH = blood loss of 500 ml or more after vaginal birth (1000 ml after cesarean). Primary: within 24 hours; secondary: 24 h to 6 weeks.
4 T's: Tone (atony, most common), Trauma (tears, rupture, inversion), Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (clotting problems).
Atony risks: over-distended uterus (twins, polyhydramnios, big baby), prolonged or rapid labor, grand multipara, oxytocin use, infection.
Soft uterus → atony. Firm uterus with bleeding → look for tears.
Call for help; massage the uterus until firm; empty the bladder.
Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV, then infusion (20 IU in 1 L); ergometrine (if no hypertension) or misoprostol 800 mcg.
Two large IV lines, fluids, cross-match blood; monitor vital signs and blood loss.
Check placenta completeness and look for tears; bimanual compression if bleeding continues.
Prevention: AMTSL for every woman.
A woman bleeds heavily after delivery and her uterus is soft and boggy. What is the first nursing action?
a. Massage the fundus ✓: stimulates contraction to control atonic bleeding.
b. Pack the vagina ✗: does not treat atony.
c. Give ergometrine without checking BP ✗: check for hypertension first; massage comes first.
d. Place her in Trendelenburg and wait ✗: does not stop bleeding.
On day 4 after cesarean for prolonged labor a mother has fever 38.8 °C, lower abdominal pain, tender uterus and foul-smelling lochia.
Puerperal morbidity: temperature 38 °C or more on any 2 of the first 10 days postpartum (excluding the first 24 hours).
Endometritis: fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia, subinvolution → antibiotics.
Risks: cesarean, prolonged labor, prolonged ROM, many vaginal exams, manual placenta removal, anemia.
Mastitis: fever, chills, red, hot, tender area of one breast; caused by milk stasis and cracked nipples.
Endometritis: IV antibiotics, fluids, semi-Fowler's (drains lochia), perineal hygiene.
Mastitis: CONTINUE breastfeeding or express milk, start on the affected side, warm compress, rest, fluids, analgesia, antibiotics.
Prevent: correct latch, frequent feeds, hand hygiene, limit vaginal exams.
A breastfeeding mother has a red, hot, tender area on one breast and fever. What should the nurse advise?
a. Stop breastfeeding from that breast ✗: milk stasis worsens mastitis.
b. Continue breastfeeding or express milk, apply warm compresses and take antibiotics as ordered ✓: emptying the breast resolves stasis.
c. Bind the breasts tightly ✗: used for suppressing lactation, not mastitis.
d. Apply cold only and wait ✗: milk must be removed.
On day 3 a new mother cries easily, feels irritable and anxious, but cares for her baby well.
Blues: 50–70% of mothers, first 2 weeks, crying, mood swings; resolves by about day 10 without drugs.
Depression: 10–15%, weeks to months; hopelessness, insomnia, loss of interest, poor bonding, inability to cope.
Psychosis: rare (0.1–0.2%), hallucinations, delusions, risk of harming self or baby → emergency.
Refer urgently if suicidal or harmful thoughts, hallucinations, lack of interest in the baby.
Blues: support, reassurance, rest, involve family.
Depression: counseling, antidepressants; screen at postnatal visits.
Psychosis: do not leave mother alone with the baby; psychiatric admission.
A mother 2 weeks after birth hears voices telling her the baby is evil. What is the priority?
a. Reassure her it is postpartum blues ✗: hallucinations are not blues.
b. Ensure the safety of mother and baby and refer urgently to psychiatry ✓: postpartum psychosis is an emergency.
c. Encourage more rest at home ✗: inadequate for psychosis.
d. Teach breastfeeding technique ✗: not the priority.

notes.title: Abnormal uterine bleeding: name the pattern

lines.text: A 45-year-old has heavy periods lasting 9 days every month and a bulky uterus.
Menorrhagia: heavy or long periods (fibroids, IUD, hyperplasia).
Metrorrhagia: bleeding between periods (polyps, cancer).
Polymenorrhea: cycles shorter than 21 days. Oligomenorrhea: cycles longer than 35 days.
Menometrorrhagia: irregular, heavy bleeding.
Postcoital (contact) bleeding = cervical cancer until proven otherwise.
Postmenopausal bleeding needs endometrial biopsy to exclude cancer.
Dysfunctional bleeding is a diagnosis after excluding pregnancy, cancer and other causes.
Always rule out pregnancy first; check Hgb; treat with hormones (COC, progestin), D&C, ablation or hysterectomy as needed.
A 38-year-old reports bleeding after intercourse. What must be ruled out first?
a. Normal ovulation bleeding ✗: not a cause of contact bleeding.
b. Cervical cancer ✓: postcoital bleeding is cervical cancer until proven otherwise.
c. Menopause ✗: she is 38 and bleeding is linked to intercourse.
d. Constipation ✗: unrelated.
A 22-year-old with multiple partners has lower abdominal pain, fever, purulent discharge, pain during intercourse, and cervical motion tenderness.
PID = infection of the upper genital tract: endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, peritonitis.
Mostly sexually transmitted: gonorrhea and chlamydia; also after abortion, delivery, IUD insertion.
Minimum signs: lower abdominal tenderness + adnexal tenderness + cervical motion tenderness.
Always do a pregnancy test: exclude ectopic pregnancy.
Complications: infertility (tubal blockage), ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, abscess.
Outpatient: ceftriaxone (or spectinomycin) + doxycycline 14 days + metronidazole 14 days; admit if no improvement in 72 h, pregnant, or very ill.
Treat the partner; no sex until both finish treatment; condoms; test for HIV and syphilis.
Priority nursing diagnosis: acute pain; semi-Fowler's helps drainage.
Doxycycline is not given in pregnancy.
A woman has lower abdominal pain, fever and cervical motion tenderness. What is the most important complication to prevent through prompt treatment?
a. Cervical cancer ✗: PID does not directly cause cervical cancer.
b. Infertility and ectopic pregnancy from tubal damage ✓: scarred tubes are the main long-term harm.
c. Menopause ✗: unrelated.
d. Fibroids ✗: not caused by infection.

notes.title: Abortion types: which one is it?

lines.text: At 10 weeks a woman has heavy bleeding with clots, cramping, and the cervix is open with tissue felt in the os.
Abortion = loss before viability (28 weeks in Ethiopia, about 500 g).
Threatened: light bleeding, mild cramps, cervix CLOSED, fetus alive → may continue.
Inevitable (imminent): heavy bleeding, painful contractions, cervix OPEN, nothing passed yet.
Incomplete: some tissue passed, cervix OPEN, bleeding continues → evacuate (MVA/D&E).
Complete: all tissue passed, cervix CLOSED, bleeding settling.
Missed: fetus dead but retained, uterus small for dates, no FHR; risk of DIC.
Septic: fever, foul discharge, tender uterus, often after unsafe abortion → IV antibiotics + evacuation.
Recurrent: 3 or more consecutive losses; painless 2nd trimester loss → cervical incompetence.
Threatened: rest, avoid sex, follow-up ultrasound.
Inevitable/incomplete: IV line, oxytocin or ergometrine, evacuation, blood if needed.
Give anti-D to Rh-negative women.
A woman at 8 weeks has light bleeding and mild cramps; the cervix is closed and ultrasound shows a live fetus. What is the diagnosis?
a. Inevitable abortion ✗: the cervix would be open.
b. Threatened abortion ✓: bleeding with closed cervix and live fetus.
c. Incomplete abortion ✗: tissue passed and open cervix.
d. Missed abortion ✗: the fetus would be dead.
A 17-year-old who was raped asks about ending her pregnancy at 9 weeks.
Ethiopian law allows termination for: rape or incest, danger to the mother's life or health, serious fetal anomaly, mother physically or mentally unable to raise the child (and minors).
Unsafe abortion = untrained provider or unhygienic setting: a major cause of maternal death.
1st trimester methods: manual vacuum aspiration, medical (mifepristone then misoprostol).
Complications: hemorrhage, infection, uterine perforation, Rh isoimmunization.
Counsel without judgment; keep confidentiality; offer post-abortion contraception and anti-D if Rh negative.
For rape survivors also: emergency contraception if early, HIV PEP within 72 hours, STI prophylaxis, psychological support.
Under Ethiopian law, which situation allows legal termination of pregnancy?
a. Pregnancy resulting from rape ✓: rape and incest are legal grounds.
b. Wanting a baby of a different sex ✗: not a legal ground.
c. Partner refuses to marry ✗: not a legal ground.
d. Pregnancy at 35 weeks for convenience ✗: not allowed.
A woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhea and past PID collapses with severe one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder pain, pulse 124, BP 80/50.
Implantation outside the uterus; 95% in the fallopian tube (mostly ampulla).
Risks: previous PID/salpingitis, previous ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD, smoking.
Classic triad: amenorrhea + vaginal bleeding/spotting + abdominal pain.
Rupture: sudden severe pain, shoulder-tip pain (blood under the diaphragm), fainting, shock, distended tender abdomen.
Differential: threatened abortion, PID, ruptured/twisted ovarian cyst, appendicitis.
Ruptured: treat shock (2 IV lines, cross-match), prepare for immediate laparotomy (salpingectomy).
Unruptured and stable: methotrexate or conservative surgery if fertility matters.
Anti-D for Rh-negative women.
A woman with 6 weeks amenorrhea has sudden severe pelvic pain, shoulder pain, and BP 85/50. What is the priority?
a. Give analgesics and observe ✗: she is in shock from probable rupture.
b. Resuscitate and prepare for emergency laparotomy ✓: ruptured ectopic needs urgent surgery.
c. Schedule ultrasound next week ✗: dangerous delay.
d. Start methotrexate ✗: only for unruptured, stable ectopic.
A 48-year-old with many births has postcoital bleeding and foul yellow discharge. A cervical mass bleeds on contact.
Most common gynecologic cancer worldwide in developing countries; caused by high-risk HPV (16, 18).
Risks: early sexual debut, multiple partners, high parity, smoking, HIV, low socioeconomic status.
Signs: postcoital, intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding; foul discharge; contact-bleeding cervical mass; pelvic pain, anemia late.
Screening: VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid), Pap smear, HPV test; biopsy confirms.
Precancer (CIN 2–3): cryotherapy, LEEP, cone biopsy. Invasive cancer: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy.
Prevention: HPV vaccine for girls (bivalent 16/18 or quadrivalent 6/11/16/18), screening, condoms.
5-year survival: stage 1 about 75%, stage 2 55%, stage 3 30%, stage 4 7%.
Follow-up 2–6 weeks after treatment; counsel about regular screening.
What is the main cause of cervical cancer?
a. Herpes simplex virus ✗: not the main cause.
b. High-risk human papillomavirus (types 16 and 18) ✓: persistent infection causes most cervical cancers.
c. Candida infection ✗: not carcinogenic.
d. Oral contraceptive use alone ✗: a minor factor only.
A 58-year-old nulliparous woman has abdominal bloating, early fullness, weight loss and a pelvic mass.
Highest death rate of gynecologic cancers because it is found late.
Risk: age over 40, nulliparity, infertility, family history, breast/endometrial cancer.
Protective: pregnancy, breastfeeding, oral contraceptive use.
Vague symptoms: bloating, abdominal swelling, constipation, weight loss; pelvic mass on exam.
Diagnosis: ultrasound, surgery; treatment: surgery, chemotherapy.
Which factor protects against ovarian cancer?
a. Nulliparity ✗: a risk factor.
b. Long-term oral contraceptive use ✓: suppressing ovulation lowers risk.
c. Family history ✗: a risk factor.
d. Age over 60 ✗: a risk factor.
A couple has had regular unprotected sex for 14 months without pregnancy. The wife had PID before.
Infertility: no conception after 1 year of regular unprotected sex. Primary = never pregnant; secondary = pregnant before.
Female causes: ovulation problems, tubal damage (PID, chlamydia), uterine problems (fibroids, adhesions), cervical factors.
Evaluate BOTH partners; semen analysis is a first-line test.
Clomiphene induces ovulation (pregnancy about 40%, twins about 5%).
A woman has never conceived after 18 months of trying. What is this called?
a. Secondary infertility ✗: means she had a previous pregnancy.
b. Primary infertility ✓: never pregnant after 1 year of trying.
c. Sterility ✗: means permanent inability to conceive.
d. Recurrent abortion ✗: requires pregnancy losses.
A 60-year-old grand multipara feels something coming down from the vagina, worse on standing and straining.
Weak pelvic floor after many births, prolonged labor, aging → organs bulge into the vagina.
Cystocele (bladder, front wall), rectocele (rectum, back wall), enterocele (bowel), uterine prolapse.
Mild: Kegel exercises, pessary. Severe: surgery.
Teach Kegel exercises: tighten pelvic floor muscles as if stopping urine, hold 10 seconds, repeat many times daily.
Which exercise helps a woman with mild uterine prolapse?
a. Sit-ups ✗: increase abdominal pressure.
b. Kegel (pelvic floor) exercises ✓: strengthen pelvic support.
c. Heavy lifting ✗: worsens prolapse.
d. Running long distances ✗: increases downward pressure.
